title: Kamtza and Bar Kamtza (Gittin 55b–56a)
hook: a wrong invitation and a public shaming; the Talmud ties Jerusalem's fall to it

segments.voice: Yesterday four sages entered the orchard, and only Akiva came out whole. Your line was enter in peace, leave in peace.

An invitation goes to the wrong person. A group text, the wrong contact, two people with almost the same name. Usually it's awkward for a minute and then everyone laughs. The Talmud tells of an invitation sent to the wrong man, and a host who didn't laugh. It happened, the story says, in Jerusalem, near the end of the days of the Second Temple. And the Talmud opens it with a startling sentence: because of Kamtza and Bar Kamtza, Jerusalem was destroyed.
screen: `THE WRONG CONTACT.` → `A HOST WHO DIDN'T LAUGH.` → `BECAUSE OF KAMTZA AND BAR KAMTZA.`

segments.voice: Tractate Gittin tells it. A man had a friend named Kamtza and an enemy named Bar Kamtza. He threw a feast and told his servant: bring me Kamtza. The servant brought Bar Kamtza. The host found his enemy at his table and said: get out. Bar Kamtza said: since I'm here, let me stay, and I'll pay for what I eat. No. I'll pay for half the feast. No. I'll pay for the whole feast. No. And the host took him by the hand and threw him out in front of everyone. Here's the line that stings: the rabbis were sitting right there, and they didn't say a word. Bar Kamtza thought: if they sat and didn't stop it, they must have been fine with it. In his humiliation he went to the Roman authorities, told them the Jews were rebelling, and set up a test that led to war. The story goes on, and it's complicated. But the Talmud's point is clear. A city fell because of a public shaming, and because the people who could have stopped it stayed silent. Historians describe many causes for Rome's destruction of Jerusalem: politics, war, empire. The Talmud isn't writing that kind of history. It's asking a different question: what went wrong inside us? Its answer is small and uncomfortable. It began at a dinner party.
screen: `THE WRONG GUEST.` · `I'LL PAY FOR THE WHOLE FEAST.` · `THE RABBIS SAID NOTHING.` · `WHAT WENT WRONG INSIDE US?` · then, large: `SHAME DESTROYS CITIES.`

segments.voice: Picture where you'll be today, a meeting, a group chat, a family dinner, and someone there who's easy to embarrass or often gets made fun of. See yourself not being the one who shames them, and, if someone else does, being the one who doesn't stay silent. One quiet sentence is enough: hey, let's not.
Bar Kamtza, thrown out of a feast after a wrong invitation, while the rabbis watching stayed silent. The Talmud ties Jerusalem's fall to it.
Your line: shame destroys cities. So can the silence of the people standing around it. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The story of Kamtza and Bar Kamtza is often taught in the weeks before Tisha b'Av, the fast mourning the Temples' destruction, along with the Talmud's teaching that the Second Temple fell because of baseless hatred.

match.prompt: who's who in the story — tap the pairs.
pairs: the host's enemy, invited by mistake

myth: Bar Kamtza offered to pay for the whole feast to stay
the host refused and threw him out anyway.
the rabbis at the feast protested
they said nothing, and Bar Kamtza took their silence as approval.
the Talmud's story is meant as a full military history
it asks what went wrong inside the community, not how the war was fought.

fork.setup: you're a guest at the feast. the host is throwing out a man who offered to pay for everything. what do you do?
options: stay quiet. it's not your party.
fork.reveal: in the story the rabbis stayed silent, and the Talmud counts their silence as part of what went wrong.

original.note: Hebrew: baseless hatred, the Talmud's name for what brought down the Second Temple.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a party.
what it means: public shame, and silence around it, can bring down a whole community.
what a scholar hears: Gittin 55b–56a is the Talmud's moral reading of the destruction, and Yoma 9b names baseless hatred as the cause.
guess: the man shamed at a feast he was invited to by mistake
the host's close friend, the guest who was meant to come
a rabbi who stayed silent while a guest was thrown out

notes: Gittin 55b–56a paraphrased. The script summarizes the rest (the blemished calf, Rabbi Zechariah ben Avkulas) as 'set up a test that led to war'; a Keeper may want it told.
A parallel is in Eichah Rabbah 4:3; please confirm the reference.
Care with history: the script attributes Jerusalem's destruction in 70 CE to Rome and presents the Talmud's story as a moral reading, not history.
Informing to Rome: the script says 'went to the Roman authorities' without stereotyping.
